title: Macedonian court jails 33 ethnic Albanians over 2015 shootout
text: A court in Macedonia on Thursday handed jail terms to 33 ethnic Albanians, seven of them life sentences, after finding them guilty of plotting attacks and clashing with police in a 2015 shootout that killed 22 people. The 33 had been accused of belonging to a group of Albanian gunmen involved in the May 9, 2015 shootout with police in Kumanovo, a town in northern Macedonia, in which eight police officers were among the dead and dozens were wounded. Some of the defendants came from neighboring Kosovo, while others belonged to Macedonia's own Albanian minority. The evidence presented by the prosecutor shows that the accused committed the criminal acts of terrorism and terrorist organization, the presiding judge said. The court was under heavy police protection, with helicopters flying overhead. The defendants protested as the verdict was read out, leading the judge to order 33 of them out of the courtroom before the sentences were heard. The 2015 shootout took place during a police raid that followed an attack by armed men on a border post. Some of the attackers were former guerrillas from the National Liberation Army (NLA), an ethnic Albanian militia that fought an insurgency in 2001 in which scores of people were killed. The NLA disbanded in 2002, and some of its former leaders went on to join the government. Naser Raufi, one of the defense lawyers, said the trial had been staged and that he had not expected such lengthy sentences. This calls for an independent investigation, he said. Macedonia, a small former Yugoslav republic of about two million people, declared independence in 1991 and largely escaped the violence that accompanied the break-up of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, until the clashes with ethnic Albanian fighters in 2001.

title: Study: Trump-backed Navy expansion would add some $400 billion in costs over 30 years
text: Growing the U.S. Navy to 355 ships, as military leaders have recommended and President Donald Trump has backed, would cost some $400 billion more over the next 30 years than the 308-ship fleet currently planned, a study released on Monday found. Building, crewing and operating a 355-ship fleet would cost about $102 billion a year, or 13 percent more than the $90 billion required for the Navy as currently planned, according to the study by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. That $102 billion price tag for the 355-ship fleet is 33 percent higher than what Congress appropriated in 2016 for the current 275-ship Navy, the CBO said. Reaching the larger force would require $26.6 billion a year for ship construction, 60 percent more than the average Congress has appropriated for shipbuilding over the past 30 years, the CBO study said. The Navy's 2017 shipbuilding plan called for increasing the fleet to 308 ships, which was expected to cost $21.2 billion a year to carry out over 30 years. After Trump pushed during last year's presidential campaign to expand the fleet to 350 ships, the Navy released a new force structure assessment in December calling for a 355-ship Navy. Allowing for the retirement of older ships, building a 355-ship fleet would mean the Navy buying about 329 new ships over 30 years, compared with 254 under its earlier plan for a 308-ship fleet, the CBO study found. Under the larger fleet plan the Navy would need to buy about 12 ships a year, against about eight a year under the earlier plan. The bigger fleet would also need more civilian and uniformed personnel and more aircraft, driving up overall operating costs, the CBO said.

title: Fox News Appoints 2 Insiders to Top Posts
text: When he took over the leadership of Fox News last month, Rupert Murdoch promised a fresh start at a network reeling from accusations that Roger Ailes, its longtime chairman, had presided over a culture of harassment and intimidation. title: At Elie Wiesel's Funeral, a Legacy Remembered Beyond His Moral Voice
text: Elie Wiesel's funeral, held on Sunday at a synagogue on Manhattan's Upper East Side, was a gathering of his family and close friends. But outside on East 62nd Street stood people, some of them in tears, who had never met the man who survived the Holocaust to become a clarion voice for the victims who did not. “He was someone who protected us he interceded against our worst instincts,” said Sarah Bardin, 44, a preschool teacher who had come to pay her respects, crying as she spoke. She knew Mr. Wiesel, who died on Saturday at 87, only through his prolific writing. His works, among them the memoir “Night,” gave voice to the Jews murdered in World War II and insisted they never be forgotten. Without him, Ms. Bardin said, the world felt like a more vulnerable place. Inside the Orthodox Fifth Avenue Synagogue, about 100 people attended a ceremony that not only reflected on Mr. Wiesel as a man of extraordinary scholarship and influence who won a Nobel Peace Prize for his life's work, but also remembered him as a friend, a mentor, a husband, a father and a grandfather. His widow, Marion, listened from a wheelchair as Mr. Wiesel was eulogized by his son Elisha, a partner at Goldman Sachs. He described growing up with a man of such stature who still had time for unconditional love. A young grandson, Elijah, spoke of sharing simple moments with a man who was a moral titan to many, recalling the fun of making English muffins together, smothered in blueberry jam. Mr. Wiesel was liberated from the Buchenwald camp with the numbers tattooed on his arm.

title: What could be in Donald Trump's tax returns?
text: On 23 September 1952, Richard Nixon, then a vice presidential candidate, gave a speech setting out "everything I have earned, everything I have spent and everything I own". He ended by challenging the Democratic presidential candidate, Illinois Governor Adlai Stevenson, to do likewise. Neither Nixon nor his presidential running mate, Dwight Eisenhower, followed suit. Two decades later, however, at the height of the Watergate scandal and while under audit by the US tax authority, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), then-President Nixon published his tax returns in the hope of clearing the air. It did not work, but it established a precedent for making tax filings public. "It's proof you have nothing to hide," says Joe Thorndike, a tax historian at Tax Analyst. Donald Trump says he needs no such proof. Saying he faces an audit of his own, the presumptive Republican nominee has refused to release his tax returns, even as public pressure on him to do so grows. Every US presidential candidate since 1976 has released their tax returns, though no law requires it. Mr Trump's refusal has fuelled growing speculation about what he could possibly be hiding. "Tax returns are sort of black and white and you sign your name to say this is accurate. It's not open to interpretation," says Mr Thorndike. The first thing the public would learn is what tax rate Mr Trump pays. The candidate has boasted of paying a very low tax rate and of exploiting the complex US tax code and its many loopholes.

title: Back to Blue: UK to Drop Maroon European Passport in Favour of Iconic Dark Blue Design
text: The Home Office has confirmed that the maroon passport now held by British citizens will go back to its original dark blue colour as Britain prepares to leave the European Union. The classic dark blue design, which was replaced in 1988 to comply with the EU policy of a single European passport, could be back as soon as 2019, with a number of contractors currently bidding to produce it. In 2007, the European Union sought to dilute the passport's individuality further by insisting that the words “Her Britannic Majesty,” be removed from the first page. Tory MP Andrew Rosindell, chairman of the Parliamentary Flags and Heraldry Committee, said: “It’s a matter of identity. Having the pink European passports has been a source of humiliation. It merged us into one European identity, which isn’t what we are.” “The old dark blue design was a distinct, clear and bold statement of what it means to be British, which is just what our citizens need as they travel abroad after Brexit,” he went on. The government's current contract with passport manufacturer De La Rue expires in 2019, and the Home Office is now accepting proposals from companies to manage the £490 million redesign project. Other priorities for the government's new design will include building in new mechanisms to combat identity fraud. Responding to the news, a Home Office spokesperson said: “We are launching the procurement process now to ensure there is sufficient time to produce and design UK passports from 2019 when the current contract ends.” The British passport was an issue frequently raised by former UKIP leader Nigel Farage, who pointed out that as well as carrying the words 'European Union' on the front, it also guarantees British citizenship rights for all 500 million EU citizens.
